title: Are Diet Drinks Bad for You? | GetMacros
h1: Are diet drinks bad for you?

blocks.text: Are diet drinks bad for you?
A diet soda can be a useful swap, an ordinary preference or a habit worth changing. The evidence depends on what it replaces and what question you ask.
Published August 27, 2026 · Updated September 9, 2026 · 6 minute read · By GetMacros

Approved low- and no-calorie sweeteners are considered safe within established intake limits for most people. Replacing a sugar-sweetened drink with a diet version can reduce calories and added sugar. That does not make diet drinks necessary, nutritious or proven to improve long-term health. Water remains the simplest default; a diet drink can be one optional tool rather than the foundation of hydration.

“Is diet soda healthy?” has no useful control group. Compared with a regular soda, a diet version removes most or all of the sugar and calories. Compared with water, it adds sweetness, acidity and sometimes caffeine without providing essential nutrition. Compared with a beverage you genuinely enjoy once in a while, the difference may be too small to deserve daily anxiety.
Less sweetness and acidity; possibly less caffeine
More exposure and a stronger habit

Regulators evaluate individual sweeteners and establish acceptable daily intakes with safety margins. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration states that approved sweeteners are safe under their intended conditions of use and publishes separate intake information for compounds such as aspartame, sucralose and acesulfame potassium. Its current overview is Aspartame and Other Sweeteners in Food .

Safety does not mean unlimited intake is encouraged. It means the evidence reviewed by the regulator supports use under defined conditions. Products differ, and a person may consume a sweetener from drinks, gum, yogurt, protein products and other foods on the same day.
People with phenylketonuria (PKU) must restrict phenylalanine and should avoid or limit aspartame according to their medical plan. Products containing aspartame carry a phenylalanine warning.

In 2023, the International Agency for Research on Cancer classified aspartame as “possibly carcinogenic,” a hazard category indicating limited evidence—not a measure of risk at a typical dose. At the same time, the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives reviewed exposure and retained its acceptable daily intake of 0–40 mg per kilogram of body weight. The agencies explained the distinction in their joint hazard and risk assessment release .

The WHO example estimated that a 70 kg adult would need more than roughly 9–14 cans containing 200–300 mg of aspartame each day to exceed that intake, assuming no other sources. That example is not a target and formulations vary. It illustrates why “possibly hazardous” and “high risk at ordinary exposure” are not interchangeable.
Do diet drinks help with weight loss?

If a diet drink replaces a caloric drink and nothing else changes, energy intake falls. Controlled trials are useful here because people who already have health concerns may choose diet drinks, making observational associations difficult to interpret.

A 52-week randomized trial in adults participating in a behavioral weight-management program found that non-nutritive-sweetened beverages were not worse than water for body-weight management and produced a modestly different outcome in that specific program. A 2024 network meta-analysis of randomized beverage trials also found small average weight differences favoring low/no-calorie sweetened beverages over several comparators, including water, but the size was modest and the included interventions differed ( study abstract ).

These results do not make diet soda a fat-loss supplement. They show that, when used as a replacement, a no-calorie beverage does not automatically trigger enough compensation to erase the calorie difference in every controlled setting.
Why does WHO advise against using sweeteners for weight control?

The World Health Organization’s 2023 guideline conditionally recommends against using non-sugar sweeteners as a long-term strategy for weight control or prevention of chronic disease. The guideline emphasizes that long-term benefit is uncertain and that associations with disease in observational studies may be confounded. It also says the recommendation is not a toxicological safety assessment of individual sweeteners.

That distinction matters. The WHO non-sugar sweetener guideline asks whether a public-health strategy creates durable benefit. The FDA and JECFA safety assessments ask whether specific compounds are safe at certain exposures. A product can pass a safety review without being recommended as an essential long-term health tool.
What observational studies can and cannot tell you

Many cohort studies find that people who report more diet-drink intake also have higher rates of diabetes, cardiovascular disease or weight gain. Those associations deserve study, but they do not by themselves show that the drink caused the outcome. People at higher risk may switch from sugary drinks to diet versions; this is called reverse causation. Diet-drink users may also differ in body weight, dieting history, food pattern, smoking, medication use and other factors.

Randomized trials are better for testing a specific substitution over months. Long observational follow-up is better for finding patterns over years. Neither design is perfect, and results should not be blended into a scarier certainty than the methods support.
Teeth, caffeine and appetite still count

Removing sugar reduces one driver of tooth decay, but carbonated soft drinks can remain acidic and frequent sipping can contribute to enamel erosion. Caffeine may help alertness but can interfere with sleep or cause symptoms in sensitive people. Some people find sweet drinks increase cravings; others use them to satisfy a preference without extra calories. Individual experience belongs in the decision as long as it is not presented as universal biology.
If you drink regular soda daily: switching some servings to diet soda or water can reduce added sugar and calories. The best bridge is the one you can sustain.
If you already drink mostly water: you do not gain a health advantage by adding diet drinks.
If diet soda helps you avoid a drink you do not want: it can be a useful option without needing to become a health food.
If it crowds out water, affects sleep or keeps you constantly chasing sweetness: reducing frequency may make sense.
If you are pregnant, have PKU, react to caffeine, or have a condition affected by specific ingredients: follow individualized medical guidance and the product label.
A simple pattern is water most of the time, with coffee, tea, milk or fortified alternatives and other drinks chosen for preference and context. A can does not define the diet.
U.S. FDA: aspartame and other sweeteners — regulatory safety and acceptable intake information.
WHO guideline on non-sugar sweeteners — conditional public-health recommendation, separate from toxicological safety limits.
WHO/IARC/JECFA aspartame assessment — explains hazard versus exposure-based risk.
52-week randomized beverage trial and 2024 network meta-analysis of randomized trials — weight-management evidence under controlled substitutions.
This article addresses generally healthy adults and common low/no-calorie soft drinks. It does not evaluate every sweetener, energy drink, dental condition or individual response.

Diet drinks are not poison and they are not a requirement. They can be a practical lower-calorie replacement for sugary drinks. Water is still the best default for hydration, and long-term health depends far more on the overall food pattern than on whether an occasional drink says “diet” on the can.

Compare real orders for protein, calories, fiber and portion size. The best choice depends on what you want from your next meal.
Start with the meal, not the restaurant’s reputation

A chain with a useful grilled-chicken option may also sell meals that do not fit your needs. A salad can contain more calories than a sandwich once you include its dressing. Compare the exact order you want to eat.
These six examples answer different questions. They are not a ranking of every restaurant, and the smallest calorie number is not automatically the best meal.
Panda Express — Bigger Plate: fried rice + 3 grilled teriyaki chicken entrées
High protein in a small portion
Chick-fil-A: Grilled Nuggets, 12 count. This is a protein portion, not necessarily enough food for lunch. Add a side if you want more energy or fiber. Dipping sauce is separate.
Chipotle: High Protein-High Fiber Bowl. This named build includes chicken, light brown rice, black beans, vegetables and salsas. Use Chipotle’s calculator when you change ingredients.
A sandwich with a clear portion size

h1: Body recomposition: can you lose fat and build muscle?

blocks.text: Body recomposition: can you lose fat and build muscle?
Body recomposition means losing body fat while gaining muscle. It can happen, but progress is gradual and the scale may not show the full change.
Who is most likely to make progress?

Newer lifters, people returning after time away and people with more stored body fat may have more room for simultaneous changes. Experienced lifters can sometimes do it too, but there is no guarantee based on a category or body-fat percentage.
Studies have shown lean-mass gains during weight loss under specific training and nutrition conditions. Those results do not mean everyone should copy a study’s aggressive diet or training schedule.
Resistance training: follow a suitable program and make progress over time.
Enough protein: choose a daily target that fits your size and training.
Enough food: maintenance or a modest deficit may fit the goal better than a large cut.
Recovery: allow time for sleep, rest and consistent meals.
The calculator’s “Lose fat + build muscle” option gives an estimate with a smaller deficit. It cannot predict whether you personally will gain muscle at that intake.
Look at several measures together: how clothes fit, waist measurements taken consistently, training performance and weight trends. Photos are optional, not a requirement.
A smaller waist and improving strength may suggest progress, but they do not precisely measure muscle gain. Strength also changes with skill and practice. Home body-fat scales are estimates too.

Think in months rather than days. The pace depends on training history, starting point, nutrition and recovery. Stable weight can coexist with changing body composition, but stable weight alone does not prove recomposition.
When should you change the plan?

If recovery is poor or the routine is hard to maintain, review the deficit and training demands. If maximum muscle gain or faster weight loss becomes your priority, a more focused approach may be easier to assess.
Choose the approach that fits your health and daily life. You do not need to pursue both goals at once to make worthwhile progress.

title: Should You Eat the Same Calories on Rest Days? | GetMacros
h1: Should you eat the same calories on rest days?

blocks.text: Should you eat the same calories on rest days?
A rest day is still a recovery day. Your calorie pattern can change, but the weekly plan still has to add up.

Keeping calories similar every day is simple and works well for many people. Eating somewhat more on hard training days and less on rest days can also work if it improves performance or adherence. Keep protein consistent and avoid turning rest days into severe restriction.

Your body does not reset its energy accounting at midnight. Training, recovery, spontaneous movement and appetite vary across the week. That means daily calories do not have to be identical—but changing them is optional, not automatically more advanced.
Simple shopping, meal prep and tracking
May feel inflexible around unusually hard sessions
Places more carbohydrate and energy near demanding work
Rest days can become needlessly low
Allows appetite and schedule to vary while preserving the weekly direction
A wide range can become inconsistent without a plan
Why rest days still need food

Exercise creates a recovery demand that continues after the session. Muscle remodeling, glycogen restoration and the rest of daily life do not stop because the calendar says “rest.” Research in endurance-trained men has even found that protein requirements may remain substantial on recovery days. That single study does not set everyone’s target, but it is a useful reminder not to treat recovery as inactivity.

Keep your daily protein target broadly consistent unless a qualified professional has given you a different plan. Recovery continues between workouts, and a predictable protein pattern is easier to execute.

For fat loss, the overall deficit needs to be tolerable and sustained. For muscle gain, keep the surplus consistent with your training plan. Maintenance leaves the most room to follow hunger and routine.
Do not remove vegetables, fruit or satisfying meals to force an arbitrary low-day number. A plan that makes rest days miserable often creates a rebound later.
When calorie cycling may be useful
You have long or high-volume sessions that clearly feel better with more carbohydrate.
Your appetite is reliably higher on training days and lower on rest days.
You prefer a larger pre- and post-workout food budget.
Your weekly target remains clear and the pattern does not trigger restrict-and-overeat behavior.
When the same target may be better
You value predictable meal prep and grocery shopping.
Your training-day and rest-day activity are not dramatically different.
Frequent target changes make tracking harder.
You notice that “low days” worsen mood, recovery or your relationship with food.
A simple way to set the week

Start with the daily estimate from the free macro calculator . Keep it consistent for two or three weeks while watching body-weight trend, training quality, hunger and adherence. Only add calorie cycling when you can name the problem it solves.

If you do cycle, move a modest amount rather than inventing two completely different diets. Many people shift mostly carbohydrate because it directly supports demanding training, while protein stays similar. The weekly average should still reflect cutting, maintenance or gaining.
Eat the same calories on rest days if consistency helps you; vary them if the variation has a clear purpose. Neither pattern compensates for a weekly intake that does not match the goal.

title: Calories vs. Macros: What Matters More? | GetMacros
h1: Calories vs. macros: what matters more?

blocks.text: Calories vs. macros: what matters more?
Calories describe how much energy you eat. Macros describe where most of that energy comes from. Your goal helps you decide which numbers to focus on.
Published August 27, 2026 · Updated September 8, 2026 · 7 minute read · By GetMacros

For gaining or losing body weight, total energy intake matters first. For muscle retention, training performance, fullness and how a diet feels, macronutrients matter too. You do not need to choose a team: set a realistic calorie range, include enough protein and fat, then let carbohydrate and fat flex around preference and activity.
Calories and macros are not competing systems

A calorie is a unit of energy. Protein, carbohydrate and fat are macronutrients that provide most food energy. Using the conventional label factors, protein and carbohydrate provide about 4 calories per gram and fat provides about 9. Alcohol supplies about 7 calories per gram but is not an essential macronutrient.

Labels may not match perfectly because of fiber, sugar alcohols, rounding and measurement rules. The guide to label rounding explains why a small mismatch is normal.

Body weight changes over time in response to the relationship between energy intake and energy expenditure. The body is dynamic: expenditure changes with body size, activity, adaptation and other factors, so a fixed “3,500 calories equals one pound” shortcut is not a precise timeline.

The NIH Body Weight Planner uses a dynamic model because the calories needed to reach and maintain a goal change as weight changes. The practical lesson is that no macro ratio can guarantee fat loss if it does not lead to a sustained energy deficit, and no “clean” food list overrides total intake.

That does not make calories the only thing that matters. Two diets with the same mathematical energy can differ in hunger, nutrient density, protein, fiber, training quality and enjoyment—all of which affect whether a person can continue.
Protein changes what the plan supports

Protein supplies amino acids used throughout the body. During resistance training, adequate protein supports muscle repair and growth. During weight loss, it can help preserve lean tissue, especially when paired with training. Protein-rich foods may also improve fullness for many people.

A large meta-analysis found that protein supplementation produced small additional improvements in muscle and strength during resistance training, with the average fat-free-mass benefit leveling around 1.6 grams per kilogram per day . That is a research estimate for maximizing training outcomes, not a universal requirement.

If you only track one macro, protein is often the most useful candidate for a muscle-building or cutting goal. The daily protein guide shows baseline and training-oriented ranges without pretending everyone needs bodybuilder numbers.
Carbohydrate affects the work you can do

Carbohydrate is the most direct dietary source for replenishing glycogen used in moderate- and high-intensity activity. Someone doing long endurance sessions, high-volume lifting or repeated field sport usually has a stronger reason to prioritize carbohydrate than someone with a low activity level.

Low-carbohydrate eating can still produce weight loss when it creates an energy deficit, and some people prefer it. The trade-off is that very low intake may make high-volume training, food variety or social eating harder. Carbohydrate quality also matters: beans, fruit, whole grains and vegetables bring fiber and micronutrients that a gram target alone cannot show.
Fat is not a leftover macro

Dietary fat provides essential fatty acids, supports absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, adds flavor and is energy-dense. A plan that pushes fat extremely low to make room for more protein and carbohydrate can be difficult to sustain and may crowd out useful foods.

Because fat has more than twice the calories per gram of protein or carbohydrate, portions can change an energy total quickly. That is a reason to measure oils or spreads when accuracy matters—not a reason to fear them. The daily fat guide explains useful ranges and food choices.
Which matters most for each goal?
Adequate protein and carbohydrate for training
Protein adequacy, fiber, fat quality and variety
Why “hitting macros” can still miss the point

A person can technically hit protein, carbohydrate and fat targets using a narrow set of ultra-processed foods and miss variety, fiber or key micronutrients. Another person can eat highly nutritious foods but consume portions that do not support their weight goal. Numbers describe important features; they do not replace the food.
Enough food, not too much or too little for the goal.
Carbohydrate matched to activity and preference.
Fiber, fruits, vegetables and food variety.
Timing and fine detail only when they solve a real problem.
Do you need to track both?

No. Tracking can teach portion awareness, but it is not the only route to a consistent diet. Some people do well with a calorie range and protein target. Others use repeatable meals, hand-size portions or a plate framework. People with a history of disordered eating may be better served by non-numeric support.

If you want an estimate, the free macro calculator provides calories, protein, fat and carbohydrate with the assumptions shown. Treat the result as a starting range. Compare your real trend, hunger, training and recovery over several weeks before making a small adjustment.
Estimate maintenance calories; do not treat the number as a lab measurement.
Choose lose, maintain, gain or recomposition.
Set a protein range appropriate for your goal and health context.
Include fat-rich foods such as olive oil, nuts, seeds or oily fish.
Split remaining energy between carbohydrate and fat according to training and preference.
Build meals from foods you can afford, enjoy and repeat.
Review the trend, not one day.
For restaurant meals, select the calorie range and one or two priorities in Fast-food meal finder . That keeps the decision focused instead of demanding a perfect four-number match.
Why two plans with the same calories can feel different

Consider two hypothetical 2,000-calorie plans. Plan A has 100 g protein, 250 g carbohydrate and about 67 g fat. Plan B has 150 g protein, 200 g carbohydrate and about 67 g fat. Using 4 calories per gram of protein and carbohydrate and 9 per gram of fat, each comes to approximately 2,000 calories; the small difference is rounding.

Moving 50 g from carbohydrate to protein keeps the arithmetic similar but changes the foods and portions needed. This does not prove that Plan B is better. The useful question is whether either plan suits the person’s protein needs, activity, food preferences and health context.

You do not need to optimize every number at once. If you are struggling to follow a plan, first identify the actual problem: hunger, inconvenient meals, an unrealistic target, training fatigue or inaccurate portions. A more complicated macro ratio is not automatically the solution.

The NIDDK Body Weight Planner explains why energy needs change over time. Revisit estimates as circumstances change, and use a repeatable eating pattern rather than treating a calculator result as permanent.
NIH/NIDDK Body Weight Planner — dynamic modeling of calorie and activity changes over time.
NIDDK guidance on eating and activity for weight management — emphasizes a sustainable food pattern and calorie reduction for weight loss.
Morton et al. protein and resistance-training meta-analysis — long-term muscle and strength outcomes.
Systematic review of protein during energy deficit — higher protein can help mitigate lean-mass loss in demanding energy deficits.
Energy and macro needs vary with age, body size, activity, pregnancy, growth, illness and medications. This article is for general education, not a clinical nutrition prescription.

Calories decide the size of the energy budget. Macros influence what the budget supports and how livable it feels. Start with the calorie direction, protect protein and dietary fat, use carbohydrate to support the life and training you actually do, and stop before precision becomes the whole point of eating.

title: Can You Build Muscle in a Calorie Deficit? | GetMacros
h1: Can you build muscle in a calorie deficit?

blocks.text: Can you build muscle in a calorie deficit?
Possible does not mean equally likely for everyone—or optimal for maximizing muscle gain.

Some people can gain lean mass while losing fat, especially newer or returning lifters and people with more body fat. Resistance training and adequate protein matter, but larger energy deficits generally make lean-mass gains harder.

Building muscle requires a training signal, amino acids and enough recovery. Stored body energy can help cover an intake deficit, so fat loss and lean-mass gain are not biologically incompatible. But an energy deficit makes the environment less favorable for maximizing growth.

A meta-analysis found that energy deficiency impaired lean-mass gains from resistance training even when strength gains remained possible. It also found a relationship between larger deficits and poorer lean-mass outcomes. That is a reason to avoid treating an extreme cut as a muscle-building shortcut.
New lifters: the training stimulus is novel, leaving more room for early adaptation.
People returning after time off: previously built muscle may return more readily than entirely new tissue is gained.
People with more stored body fat: more stored energy is available while training creates a reason to retain or build lean tissue.
People using a modest deficit: recovery is generally easier than during severe restriction.
Advanced, already-lean lifters usually have less room for simultaneous progress. If maximum muscle gain is the priority, maintenance or a modest surplus is often the more predictable route.
What the strongest experiment can—and cannot—show

In a four-week randomized trial, young men completed intense resistance and interval training during a large energy deficit. The higher-protein group gained more lean mass and lost more fat than the lower-protein group. That shows recomposition can occur under tightly controlled, demanding conditions.
It does not prove everyone should copy the trial’s aggressive deficit, protein intake or six-day training schedule. The intervention was short, supervised and specific.
Build the plan around four priorities
Progressive resistance training: give the body a clear reason to adapt.
Adequate daily protein: use a sensible range based on body size and training, not an unlimited target.
A manageable deficit: faster weight loss can compete with recovery and lean-mass gain.
Sleep and time: judge several weeks of strength, measurements and weight trends together.
Use the macro calculator as a starting estimate, then read body recomposition explained for a longer-term view.

title: What do carbs do in your body? | GetMacros
h1: What do carbs do in your body?

blocks.text: What do carbs do in your body?
Carbohydrates provide energy. Foods such as oats, rice, potatoes, fruit and beans can also bring fiber, vitamins and minerals to your meals.

Carbohydrates include sugars, starches and fiber. Your body digests most sugars and starches into simple sugars, including glucose. Fiber behaves differently: it is not fully digested in the small intestine, and some types are fermented by gut bacteria.
How do carbs help with exercise?

Your muscles and liver store carbohydrate as glycogen. Muscle glycogen helps fuel exercise; liver glycogen helps maintain blood glucose between meals. Carb needs tend to rise with longer or more demanding training.
A short gym session does not require the same carb strategy as an endurance event. A familiar meal with rice, potatoes, bread, oats or fruit is often a practical starting point.

The brain normally uses glucose for much of its energy. During prolonged fasting or a very-low-carbohydrate diet, it can also use ketones. The body can make glucose, so eating fewer carbs does not mean the brain stops receiving fuel.
That does not make a very-low-carb diet necessary or suitable for everyone. Your preferences, training, digestion and any medical advice matter.
How many carbs should you eat?

The adult reference range is 45–65% of calories. At 2,000 calories, that works out to about 225–325 g carbohydrate. This is a broad reference, not a requirement to match the same percentage every day.

A macro calculator may set protein and fat first, then assign the remaining calories to carbs. That can produce a different split. Use the approach that fits your needs, especially if you have been given a medical nutrition plan.
Whole grains: oats, whole-wheat bread, brown rice or barley.
Beans and lentils: carbohydrate, fiber and protein in the same food.
Fruit and vegetables: fresh, frozen and canned options can all work.
Potatoes, pasta and rice: useful meal bases; portions and additions change the meal.

title: Cutting, bulking or maintenance: what do they mean? | GetMacros
h1: Cutting, bulking or maintenance: what do they mean?

blocks.text: Cutting, bulking or maintenance: what do they mean?
Cutting means eating for weight loss. Bulking means eating to support weight gain and muscle building. Maintenance means keeping weight broadly steady.
Weight trend, strength, hunger and recovery
Broadly stable weight and a sustainable routine
Training progress and the pace of weight gain
You do not have to cycle through these phases. Maintaining your weight while improving fitness and meal habits is a valid long-term goal.

Much of the food can stay the same. For weight loss, portions or calorie-dense extras may be smaller. For weight gain, larger portions or an extra snack may help. Keep protein foods, produce and other useful nutrients in both plans.
Resistance training and adequate protein support muscle retention during weight loss and muscle growth when that is your goal. Neither outcome follows from a calorie number alone.
Should you cut or bulk first?
Start with the outcome you want and whether changing weight is appropriate for you. There is no body-fat percentage that makes the decision for everyone.

If you want to improve strength without changing weight, start around maintenance. If your priority is weight loss, use a manageable deficit. If you are training consistently and want to gain, consider a modest surplus.
Can you build muscle and lose fat together?
Sometimes. This is called body recomposition. It can be more achievable for newer or returning lifters, but results vary. A large deficit generally makes muscle gain harder.
How long should a phase last?

There is no universal deadline. Review your energy, recovery, weight trend and relationship with food. You can spend time at maintenance when that better supports your health or routine; it is not a failed diet.

Use the free macro calculator for a starting estimate, then review what actually happens over several weeks. Get personal advice if pregnancy, illness, eating-disorder recovery or another health circumstance affects the plan.

title: Does Creatine Cause Hair Loss? | GetMacros

blocks.text: The concern grew from one small study that measured a hormone—not hair. In 2025, a trial finally measured both.
Published August 27, 2026 · Updated September 9, 2026 · 6 minute read · By GetMacros

Current evidence does not show that creatine monohydrate causes hair loss. The first randomized trial to measure hair density, follicular units and hair thickness found no difference between 5 grams of creatine per day and placebo over 12 weeks. That is reassuring, but it is one modest study in resistance-trained men—not proof about every person, dose or multi-year use.
Why people connected creatine to hair loss

Androgenetic alopecia—common pattern hair loss—is influenced by genetics and androgen signaling, including dihydrotestosterone (DHT) activity in susceptible hair follicles. If a supplement reliably raised DHT, a concern about hair could be biologically plausible. But plausible is not the same as demonstrated.

The creatine rumor traces mainly to a 2009 crossover study of 20 college-aged male rugby players . Participants completed a seven-day creatine loading phase at 25 grams per day followed by 14 days at 5 grams per day. Serum testosterone did not change, while DHT rose from baseline and the DHT-to-testosterone ratio changed.

That study measured blood hormones for three weeks. It did not count shed hairs, examine follicle miniaturization, measure hair density or diagnose hair loss. Its result created a hypothesis worth testing; it did not establish that creatine made anyone bald.
Why the 2009 result was not enough
Small sample: twenty participants makes an estimate more vulnerable to chance and individual variation.
Short duration: three weeks is too short to establish the clinical course of pattern hair loss.
No hair outcomes: a hormone changed, but hair was never measured.
Loading dose: the first week used 25 grams per day, higher than the common maintenance intake of 3–5 grams.
Replication: later creatine research did not consistently reproduce a meaningful androgen increase.

A 2021 expert review summarized the literature and concluded that the evidence at that time did not indicate that creatine increased testosterone, DHT or hair loss ( Antonio et al. ). Still, the obvious gap remained: nobody had directly studied hair.

The newer randomized, double-blind trial assigned resistance-trained males aged 18–40 to 5 grams per day of creatine monohydrate or a maltodextrin placebo for 12 weeks. Forty-five were recruited and 38 completed the study. Researchers measured total testosterone, free testosterone and DHT. They also used a trichogram and FotoFinder imaging to assess hair density, follicular-unit count and cumulative hair thickness.

The study found no significant group-by-time differences in the hormone measures or hair outcomes. In plain language, the creatine group did not show worse hair density, fewer follicular units or thinner cumulative hair than placebo over the study period. The full paper is available through PubMed Central .
This was not another study inferring hair effects from a blood marker. It directly measured several features of hair and follicles while using a placebo-controlled design.
What the trial still cannot prove

One 12-week study cannot establish that no creatine user could ever notice shedding. Pattern hair loss unfolds over longer periods and is strongly influenced by genetics, age and baseline follicle sensitivity. The study was limited to men aged 18–40 who resistance trained. It did not focus only on people with a strong family history or active androgenetic alopecia, and it did not test a loading phase.

The findings are reassuring, but limited. The best direct trial found no adverse hair signal over 12 weeks at 5 grams per day. Longer and larger studies in more varied populations would increase certainty.
Anecdotes deserve care, not automatic dismissal

People sometimes report shedding after starting creatine. Their experience is real, but the timing alone cannot identify the cause. Hair shedding can reflect androgenetic alopecia, telogen effluvium after illness or stress, weight loss, low energy intake, iron or thyroid problems, medications, scalp conditions and normal fluctuation. Starting a supplement may also make someone inspect their hair more closely.

Stopping and restarting a supplement is not a controlled experiment when training, diet, stress and hair cycles change at the same time. If shedding is sudden, patchy, painful, accompanied by scalp changes or persistent, a clinician or dermatologist can investigate causes that should not be missed.

Creatine helps replenish phosphocreatine, which supports rapid energy production during repeated high-intensity efforts. It is one of the most studied sports supplements. The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements notes that creatine can improve strength and power for repeated short, intense activity and that creatine monohydrate is the most widely studied form ( consumer fact sheet ).

Common practice uses 3–5 grams per day. A loading phase can saturate muscle sooner but is not required. Initial weight gain often reflects more water stored with creatine in muscle, not rapid fat gain.
If you are worried about your hair
Do not use a supplement you do not want. Creatine can help training performance, but it is optional.
Keep the question specific. Are you seeing more hairs in the shower, visible thinning, a changing hairline or a patch? Those are not identical patterns.
Take consistent photos. Same light, angle, hairstyle and interval are more useful than daily mirror checks.
Review other changes. Illness, calorie restriction, rapid weight loss, stress and medication changes can matter.
Get qualified help for ongoing loss. A dermatologist can distinguish types of hair loss and discuss treatments. Do not start or change prescription hair-loss medication based on a supplement article.
Van der Merwe et al. (2009) — small three-week rugby-player study that measured DHT but not hair.
Lak et al. (2025) — randomized 12-week trial measuring hormones and hair-follicle outcomes.
Antonio et al. (2021) — evidence review of common creatine questions and misconceptions.
NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — creatine performance, dosing and safety overview for consumers.

Several authors in creatine research have professional connections to supplement science or industry; study design, replication and direct outcomes matter more than authority alone. This article is educational and does not diagnose hair loss.

The creatine–hair-loss claim began with an indirect, small study. The first trial to directly examine hair found no harm after 12 weeks at 5 grams per day. Longer studies would help establish whether that finding holds over time. If creatine helps your training and you want to use it, current evidence does not provide a strong reason to expect hair loss.

title: Editorial policy | GetMacros

blocks.text: Here’s how I choose sources, explain nutrition and fix mistakes on GetMacros.
GetMacros is the name I publish under. The guides are not presented as medical reviews by a doctor or registered dietitian.
I use software and AI tools to help draft, organize and check the site. I’m responsible for what I publish. Linking to a source does not mean its author endorses GetMacros.
Where do the facts come from?

Restaurant pages link to official menu information. Nutrition guides use research papers, reviews and accountable sources such as the NIH, FDA and USDA. Calculators explain their formulas and assumptions.

I explain what a study found and what it cannot tell us. A short study in one group does not show what happens to everyone over years. When a restaurant does not publish a number, I leave it blank rather than count it as zero.
What makes a page worth keeping?
A page should answer a useful question or help you make a choice. I remove repeated explanations, unsupported claims and wording that makes a simple decision harder.
There is no fixed word-count target. A working calculator needs clear instructions; a research question may need more explanation and sources.

Dates change when content is meaningfully revised. Important factual or calculation corrections appear in the public corrections log. Routine spelling, layout and link repairs do not each need an entry.
If something looks wrong, send me the page link and the sentence or result to check. A source is helpful too. I check the evidence before changing a claim.

GetMacros provides general education and estimates. It does not diagnose conditions or replace individual advice from a qualified clinician or dietitian. Medical nutrition needs can differ from the general examples here.

title: What does fat do in your body? | GetMacros
h1: What does fat do in your body?

blocks.text: What does fat do in your body?
Fat provides energy, essential fatty acids and help absorbing vitamins A, D, E and K. Both the type and amount matter.
Fat is part of cell membranes and provides a concentrated source of energy: about 9 calories per gram. Your body needs essential fatty acids from food because it cannot make them itself.
Some fat with meals helps absorb fat-soluble vitamins. You do not need to add oil to every vegetable dish if the meal already contains fat from other foods.

Unsaturated fats are found in olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocado and fish. Replacing some saturated fat with unsaturated fat can improve blood cholesterol. Adding extra oil without replacing anything also adds calories.

Saturated fat is found in foods including butter, fatty meats, cheese and coconut oil. Industrial trans fat is a separate category and should be avoided. A food’s overall role in your diet matters more than a single “good” or “bad” label.
How much fat should you eat?
The adult reference range is 20–35% of daily calories. At 2,000 calories, that is about 44–78 g fat. Divide calories from fat by 9 to convert them to grams.
This range is a planning reference, not a diagnostic cutoff. Eating outside it on one day does not mean you have a deficiency or a hormone problem.

The body uses cholesterol to make steroid hormones and can produce cholesterol itself. This does not mean that eating more fat or cholesterol will reliably raise testosterone or improve muscle growth.

Research comparing low- and higher-fat diets has reported differences in testosterone, but the studies do not establish one ideal fat intake for everyone. Total energy intake and health also matter. Persistent symptoms need clinical assessment, not a higher-fat target based on a website.
Add nuts or seeds to yogurt or oats.
Use olive oil or another unsaturated oil in cooking.
Include fish if you eat it, or plant foods such as walnuts and flaxseed.
Count dressings and sauces when comparing restaurant meals.
Fat adds flavor and energy, so a modest portion can make a meal more satisfying. There is no need to remove it just because you are managing calories.

title: How many calories should I eat a day? | GetMacros
h1: How many calories should I eat a day?

blocks.text: How many calories should I eat a day?
There is no single calorie target for everyone. Your body size, age, activity and goal help estimate a starting point.
For an illustrative 30-year-old man weighing 80 kg at 180 cm, the Mifflin–St Jeor equation gives 10 × 80 + 6.25 × 180 − 5 × 30 + 5 = 1,780 calories of estimated resting energy.

That 623-calorie difference comes from the activity assumption alone. The decimal places in a calculator cannot remove that uncertainty. Use the result as a starting estimate, then reconsider the assumption as your routine changes.
Use the free macro calculator . Equation sources and calculator limitations . This adult example is not a calorie prescription.

Maintenance is the average intake that keeps your weight broadly stable. It includes energy used at rest, daily movement, exercise and digestion. The free macro calculator estimates it from your details.
The calculator uses the Mifflin–St Jeor equation for resting energy needs, then applies an activity factor. It estimates energy use; it does not measure your metabolism.

Think about the whole day, including your job and time spent walking or sitting. Workout frequency is only a rough guide. Two people who both train three days a week may move very differently the rest of the time.
Maintain weight: start near the maintenance estimate.
Lose weight: choose a manageable reduction that still supports nutrition and daily life.
Gain weight or muscle: a modest increase may help; training matters if muscle gain is the goal.
For example, reducing an illustrative maintenance estimate of 2,200 calories by 10% gives 1,980. This shows the math, not a recommendation for every reader.
How do you know if the estimate is right?

If tracking suits you, compare your intake and weight trend over several weeks under similar conditions. Consider energy, hunger and recovery too. Water retention and menstrual-cycle changes can obscure the trend for longer than two weeks.
If the pattern consistently differs from your goal, review portions and activity before making a modest adjustment. More decimal places will not make an uncertain estimate more accurate.

It is not a suitable default for everyone. A low target can make it hard to meet nutritional needs, especially for active or larger adults. Do not use a round number from the internet as a personal prescription.
Should you add exercise calories back?

An activity-based estimate already includes some exercise. Automatically adding a watch’s exercise estimate again can double-count it. If your activity changes substantially, review the overall target instead.
Use personal clinical advice during pregnancy, illness, eating-disorder recovery or other circumstances that change your needs. The site’s weight-planning calculator is designed for adults.
The Mifflin–St Jeor resting energy equation

title: How much fiber do you need per day? | GetMacros
h1: How much fiber do you need per day?

blocks.text: How much fiber do you need per day?
Fiber helps with digestion and can support heart health. Beans, whole grains, fruit, vegetables, nuts and seeds are practical ways to get more.
How much should you aim for?

Needs vary with age, sex and energy intake. The National Academies’ adequate intakes include 25 g/day for women and 38 g/day for men aged 19–50, and 21 g and 30 g respectively after age 50. Pregnancy and breastfeeding have separate reference amounts.

Another planning reference is about 14 g per 1,000 calories. The U.S. label Daily Value is 28 g. These figures come from different reference contexts, so they are not interchangeable personal prescriptions.
Add beans or lentils to a bowl, soup or pasta dish.
Choose oats or a whole-grain cereal you enjoy.
Include fruit and vegetables across meals.
Use nuts or seeds as a topping or snack.
For an exact product, check its label. The same food can have different fiber amounts depending on portion, brand and preparation.
Does the type of fiber matter?

Different fibers have different effects. Some help with stool bulk; some form gels or are fermented by gut bacteria. A mix of plant foods is a practical starting point without tracking individual fiber types.
If a clinician has recommended a particular fiber or supplement for a condition, follow that advice rather than a general food list.
How can you get more fiber when eating out?

Look for beans, lentils, whole grains and vegetables, then compare the published fiber for the complete order. A salad is not automatically the highest-fiber option, and added fiber can also contribute to a packaged wrap’s total.
Our meal finder includes a higher-fiber preference. A missing restaurant value means unknown, not zero. Higher fiber does not automatically mean lower calories or sodium.

Try one manageable change at a time and drink enough fluid. A sudden large increase can cause gas or discomfort. You do not need to force a fixed weekly increase if your digestion responds differently.
Digestive conditions can change what is appropriate. Seek individual advice if symptoms persist or you have been told to limit certain foods.
FDA: understanding the Nutrition Facts label

title: How Much Protein Can Your Body Absorb at Once? | GetMacros
h1: How much protein can your body absorb at once?

blocks.text: How much protein can your body absorb at once?
Your body can absorb more than 30 grams at a meal. Here is how absorption differs from muscle growth, and what that means for planning meals.
Published August 27, 2026 · Updated September 9, 2026 · 6 minute read · By GetMacros

Your digestive system does not stop absorbing protein after 20, 30 or 40 grams. A larger dose takes longer to digest and its amino acids can be used for muscle, other tissues, enzymes, hormones, immune proteins or energy. A moderate serving may maximize the short-term muscle-protein-synthesis response under some test conditions, but that is not the same as an absorption ceiling or a point where every extra gram is wasted.
Three questions that get collapsed into one
When people ask how much protein the body can “use,” they may mean three different things:
How much enters the body? Digestion breaks food protein into amino acids and small peptides, which the intestine absorbs.

How much maximizes muscle protein synthesis right now? Muscle tissue responds to a meal, but the size of that response depends on body size, age, training, protein quality, the rest of the meal and what was eaten earlier.
How much helps over weeks or months? Building or preserving muscle depends on total protein, resistance training, energy intake, recovery and consistency—not one perfect feeding.
The popular “30-gram limit” treats the answer to the second question as if it answered all three.

After protein reaches the stomach and small intestine, enzymes break it down. Amino acids cross the intestinal wall and enter circulation. A mixed meal with fat, carbohydrate and fiber generally moves more slowly than an isolated whey drink, which spreads amino-acid availability over a longer period.

The body has many destinations for those amino acids. Skeletal muscle is important, but it is not the only protein-containing tissue. Amino acids also contribute to organs, connective tissue, transport proteins, enzymes and other molecules. Some can be oxidized for energy. Oxidation is not proof that the meal “failed”; metabolism continually routes nutrients according to current needs.
Where the 20–30 gram idea came from

Acute feeding studies often measured muscle protein synthesis for a few hours after participants consumed a fast-digesting protein. In several contexts, roughly 20–40 grams produced a near-maximal short-term response. Larger people, older adults and people completing more demanding whole-body training may need more to produce a comparable response.

A 2018 review by Schoenfeld and Aragon emphasized that these experiments did not establish an absorption cap. Their practical proposal was around 0.4 grams per kilogram per meal across at least four meals to reach about 1.6 g/kg/day, with room up to roughly 0.55 g/kg per meal when daily intake is higher. That is a performance-oriented distribution target, not a safety boundary.

For a 75 kg (165 lb) adult, 0.4 g/kg is 30 grams per meal. That can be a convenient anchor for four meals. It does not mean a 45-gram dinner wastes 15 grams, and it does not mean everyone needs four feedings.

A 2023 controlled tracer study gave participants either 25 or 100 grams of milk protein after resistance exercise. The 100-gram dose produced a larger and more prolonged anabolic response lasting beyond 12 hours , with more dietary amino acids incorporated into multiple protein pools. The result directly challenges the idea that the body simply discards everything above a small threshold.

The study does not prove that 100 grams in one meal is the best long-term plan. It examined an acute response in healthy young men after exercise, using milk protein and intensive laboratory measurements. A larger response over 12 hours does not automatically mean greater muscle gain over a year. It does show that the body can digest and use a very large protein serving over time.
Daily protein still matters more than perfect timing

Long-term training research asks a more useful question: what intake supports changes in muscle and strength over time? A major meta-analysis of resistance-training studies found that protein supplementation produced small additional gains and that the average benefit for fat-free mass leveled off around 1.6 g/kg/day , with uncertainty around the precise breakpoint.

That finding is often simplified too aggressively. It does not say every person needs exactly 1.6 g/kg, that more is dangerous, or that food above the breakpoint has no value. It means the studies did not detect further average muscle gain from more protein beyond that neighborhood when combined with resistance training.
For general health rather than maximizing hypertrophy, needs and priorities differ. The page How much protein do I need? separates baseline reference intakes from training-oriented ranges.
Is spreading protein across meals better?

Spreading protein can be useful because it creates several opportunities to stimulate muscle protein synthesis, makes a higher daily total easier to eat and may produce meals that feel more balanced. It is especially practical for someone who currently eats almost no protein at breakfast or lunch and most of it at dinner.

An even distribution is optional. A 2020 review found that the longer-term evidence on distribution is less decisive than acute physiology alone might suggest. At least one meal with a meaningful protein dose appears useful, while total daily intake and training remain central .
Easy way to fill a daily gap
Earlier meals may be less satisfying
What should you do in real life?

Start with the daily total that fits your goal, health context and food preferences. Then distribute it in a way you can repeat. If muscle gain is a priority, a practical meal often contains roughly 25–40 grams for an average-size adult, with body-size-based targets offering more precision. Larger servings can still contribute to your daily needs.
If breakfast has 5 grams and dinner has 80, moving some protein earlier may improve convenience and meal quality.
If you prefer two meals per day and comfortably reach an appropriate daily total, you do not need to force six feedings.
If one restaurant meal contains 60 grams, enjoy the meal. You do not need to divide it into smaller servings for absorption.
If you have kidney disease, liver disease, a metabolic condition, are pregnant, or have been given a medical protein target, use individualized clinical guidance rather than a general fitness range.
Trommelen et al. (2023): 25 g versus 100 g protein after exercise — acute tracer study; large dose produced a longer response.
Schoenfeld & Aragon (2018): per-meal protein review — explains absorption versus muscle-building use and offers a distribution framework.
Morton et al. (2018): resistance training and protein meta-analysis — long-term training evidence and the approximate 1.6 g/kg/day breakpoint.
Hudson et al. (2020): protein distribution review — evaluates whether longer-term outcomes support an even pattern.

Most detailed muscle-protein research is conducted in healthy adults, often young men, under controlled conditions. Results do not cover every age, disease state, dietary pattern or training program. This article explains research; it does not set a personal medical intake.

Your body can absorb and use more than 30 grams of protein at a meal. A moderate serving may efficiently stimulate muscle protein synthesis, but larger meals are not wasted. Hit an appropriate daily total, train if muscle is the goal, and spread protein in the pattern that makes your meals satisfying and repeatable.

title: How much protein do you need per day? | GetMacros
h1: How much protein do you need per day?

blocks.text: How much protein do you need per day?
Your protein needs depend on your body size, training and health. Use these ranges as a starting point, then choose foods that make the target practical.
These categories overlap. They are different reference points, not three rules you must add together.
What does the protein RDA mean?

The adult RDA of 0.8 g/kg is designed to cover the needs of nearly all healthy adults. It is not merely the amount that prevents severe deficiency, and it was not designed as a target for maximizing muscle gain.

People who train regularly may benefit from more. Research on resistance training found that average gains in fat-free mass leveled off around 1.6 g/kg/day, with uncertainty around that estimate. That is why practical training ranges often extend to about 2.2 g/kg.
How do you calculate your target?
Multiply your weight in kilograms by the chosen grams-per-kilogram amount. To convert pounds to kilograms, divide by about 2.2. For example, 75 kg × 1.6 g/kg = 120 g protein per day.

If using your current weight produces an unusually large or difficult target, a registered dietitian can help choose an appropriate weight basis. A goal-weight calculation is an option in some circumstances, not an automatic rule for everyone.
How much protein should you eat per meal?
Split the daily total in a way that fits your routine. A 120 g example could be three meals with 40 g each, or four with 30 g each. A larger dinner is not wasted because it exceeds 30 g.

Start with a meal that currently has little protein. Yogurt, eggs, tofu, beans, fish or chicken can help, depending on what you like. A protein shake is convenient for some people, but it is optional.
When a general range is not enough

Kidney disease, pregnancy, recovery from illness and other health circumstances can change your needs. Use advice from your clinician or dietitian instead of a general training range. More protein is not automatically better.

title: How much sodium should you have per day? | GetMacros
h1: How much sodium should you have per day?

blocks.text: How much sodium should you have per day?
Packaged foods and restaurant meals can contain a lot of sodium. Check the whole portion, then compare options that fit the meal you want.
The U.S. Daily Value is less than 2,300 mg sodium per day. WHO recommends less than 2,000 mg per day for adults. These are general limits, not amounts you need to reach.
Use an individual target if your clinician has given you one. Some medical conditions and situations involving prolonged heavy sweating need more specific guidance.
Is sodium the same as salt?
No. Table salt contains sodium and chloride. About 5 g salt contains 2,000 mg sodium. Food labels in different countries may show sodium or salt, so check the label before comparing.
How do you read sodium on a label?

Find sodium in milligrams and check the serving size. A soup with 700 mg per serving contains 1,400 mg if you eat two servings. The sodium portion calculator handles that multiplication for two foods.
% Daily Value offers a quick comparison: the FDA describes 5% DV or less as low and 20% or more as high per serving. It is a label reference, not a personal meal allowance.
How do you choose a lower-sodium restaurant meal?
Compare similar portions instead of a small side with a full meal.
Include sauces, dressings and sides in the total.
Check cured meats, cheese, soups and seasoned entrées.
Ask about a sauce separately when the restaurant can accommodate it.

Changes are not always reflected in a standard menu total. The restaurant is the best source for what can be changed and whether updated nutrition is available. Our lower-sodium filter means lower within the selected options, not suitable for every medical diet.
Does water cancel out a salty meal?
No. Drinking water does not remove the sodium from the food you ate. Return to your normal routine and use the pattern across your meals to guide future choices.

A meal cooked at home is not automatically low in sodium either. Ingredients, portions and the rest of the day still count. If you have a prescribed sodium limit, follow it rather than using this general guide.

title: How to Build a Balanced Meal With Macros | GetMacros
h1: How to build a balanced meal with macros

blocks.text: How to build a balanced meal with macros
Use macros to shape the meal, not to turn dinner into an accounting exercise.

Start with a useful protein source, add a carbohydrate that fits the meal, include fruit or vegetables, and use fats and flavor deliberately. Change portion sizes for your goal instead of inventing separate ‘diet foods.’
This is a flexible assembly method, not a rule that every plate must look identical. A bean burrito, salmon rice bowl, lentil curry and yogurt-oat breakfast can all satisfy it in different ways.

Pick a serving that makes a meaningful contribution to your daily target: poultry, fish, eggs, dairy, tofu, tempeh, beans, lentils or another food you enjoy. USDA MyPlate emphasizes variety because different protein foods bring different nutrients.
2. Add carbohydrate for energy and satisfaction

Rice, potatoes, oats, bread, pasta, fruit, corn, beans and other carbohydrate foods can support training and make a meal satisfying. The amount can rise on higher-energy days and shrink on lower-energy days without labeling the food itself good or bad.
3. Add produce for volume, fiber and variety

Use vegetables or fruit that fit the meal rather than forcing a plain side salad everywhere. Frozen, canned and fresh options can all work. Sauces and preparation affect calories and sodium, so include them in the meal rather than pretending they do not count.
4. Use fat and flavor on purpose

Oil, nuts, seeds, avocado, cheese and sauces can add flavor and energy. They are especially useful when appetite is low or calories are high. During a cut, measure calorie-dense additions often enough to understand the portion—but do not strip every meal of flavor.
Adjust the same meal for three goals
Keep the protein anchor, use plenty of produce and reduce the most calorie-dense extras first.
Use portions that leave energy, hunger and weight trend broadly stable.
Add carbohydrate, a larger protein portion when needed, and convenient energy from fats or drinks.
Five meals built from the template
Chicken or tofu, rice, roasted vegetables and tahini sauce.
Lentil pasta, tomato sauce, vegetables and parmesan or nutritional yeast.
Salmon, potatoes, green beans and olive-oil dressing.
A burrito bowl with beans, rice, meat or sofritas, salsa and guacamole.
When eating out, use the same logic: identify the protein, carbohydrate, produce and calorie-dense extras, then compare the published numbers in Fast-food meal finder .

title: How to calculate your macros by hand | GetMacros
h1: How to calculate your macros by hand

blocks.text: How to calculate your macros by hand
Estimate daily calories first, then convert protein, fat and carbs into grams. This worked example explains the arithmetic behind a macro plan.
The Mifflin–St Jeor equation uses weight in kilograms, height in centimeters and age in years. It estimates resting energy expenditure.
For a 32-year-old woman weighing 68 kg at 165 cm, the estimate is 1,390.25 calories per day at rest.
2. Account for activity and your goal
Multiply resting energy by an activity factor. The site offers factors from 1.2 to 1.9. These are rough categories, not measurements; include activity outside the gym.

Using 1.55 in this example gives about 2,155 calories for maintenance. An illustrative 20% reduction gives about 1,724 calories. The factor and reduction are assumptions for this example, not instructions for everyone.
Protein provides about 4 calories per gram. If this example uses 136 g protein, it accounts for 544 calories. Choose your own amount using your needs and the daily protein guide.
Fat provides about 9 calories per gram. Choosing 28% of the example’s calories gives about 483 calories from fat, or roughly 54 g. The adult fat reference range is 20–35% of total energy.
Subtract protein and fat calories from the total, then divide by 4. Here, (1,724 − 544 − 483) ÷ 4 gives about 174 g carbohydrate.

The rounded example is 1,724 calories, 136 g protein, 54 g fat and 174 g carbs. Rounded grams may add back to a slightly different calorie total. Keep extra precision during calculation, then round the final display.
What if the numbers do not fit?
If protein and fat use more than the whole calorie target, review your assumptions. Do not force negative carbs or an impractically low calorie intake to make a formula work.
Your result is a starting estimate. Compare it with your routine and progress over time; it is not a precise measurement or a promise of a particular outcome.
The Mifflin–St Jeor resting energy equation

title: How to Calculate Maintenance Calories | GetMacros

blocks.text: A formula gives you a starting point. Your own consistent data turns it into a useful target.

Estimate resting energy needs with a validated equation, account for activity, then hold the estimate steady long enough to compare average intake with your body-weight trend. Maintenance is a working range, not one permanently exact number.

Your maintenance calories are the average intake that keeps body weight broadly stable over time. They are often called total daily energy expenditure, or TDEE. The total includes resting metabolism, movement, training and the energy used to digest food. None of those components is perfectly identical every day.
That is why maintenance is better treated as a range. A restaurant day, a long walk and a quiet workday can all have different totals while the weekly pattern remains stable.

The GetMacros calculator uses the Mifflin–St Jeor equation to estimate resting energy expenditure from weight, height, age and equation sex. The original study derived the equation from 498 healthy adults. An activity factor then converts that resting estimate into an estimated daily total.

Activity is the least precise input. “Moderately active” can mean different things to two people, and planned exercise is only part of daily movement. Use the result as a first estimate—not proof that your body burns that exact number.
Choose the calculator estimate or your current average intake as a starting point.
Keep intake reasonably consistent for two to three weeks.
Weigh under similar conditions and compare weekly averages, not isolated days.
If the average is stable, your average intake is near maintenance.
If the trend moves consistently, make a modest adjustment and observe again.
Food tracking and scale weight both contain noise. Restaurant portions vary, labels round values and body water changes quickly. More decimal places do not fix uncertain inputs.

Recheck after a meaningful weight change, a major shift in training or daily movement, or several weeks in which the trend no longer matches the plan. Energy expenditure changes with body size and composition, and it can also adapt during prolonged underfeeding. Do not react to one high or low morning.

Suppose the calculator estimates 2,450 calories. You average about 2,400 for three weeks and your weekly weight averages are 176.2, 176.0 and 176.3 pounds. That intake is probably close enough to maintenance for planning. Calling it exactly 2,413 would suggest precision the data cannot support.
Start with the free macro calculator . If your goal changes, read cutting, bulking and maintenance before changing the number.
Control of energy expenditure in humans

title: How to Calculate Calories and Macros in a Recipe
h1: How to calculate nutrition for a homemade recipe

blocks.text: How to calculate nutrition for a homemade recipe
The reliable way to estimate a homemade recipe is to calculate the whole batch first, then divide it by the finished yield or the number of equal portions.

List every meaningful source of energy or nutrients: cooking oil, sauces, milk, toppings, marinades that remain in the dish, and small ingredients that add up. Record weights when practical. Household measures are workable, but gram weights reduce ambiguity.
Match each ingredient to an entry describing the state you measured: raw, cooked, drained, canned in liquid, or dry. For branded foods, use the current package when possible.

Multiply each ingredient’s nutrients per unit by the amount used, then add the ingredients. Keep the batch total separate from serving calculations. This prevents repeated rounding and makes later portion changes easy.

After cooking, remove inedible bones or discarded liquid as appropriate and weigh the finished edible recipe in its serving container. Tare the empty container first. The finished weight captures water absorbed or evaporated during this particular cook.

For items divided into genuinely equal pieces—such as 12 muffins—counting pieces can be reasonable. Weighing the finished batch is better for soups, casseroles, curries, and dishes served in unequal scoops.

Divide the batch nutrient total by finished grams to get nutrients per gram, then multiply by the portion weight. Alternatively, divide by equal servings if you intentionally portioned the whole batch.

Do not combine raw ingredient nutrition with a cooked-food database entry for the same ingredient. Do not divide by the pre-cooking weight after substantial water change. Avoid leaving out oil because only a thin coating appears visible; estimate how much entered the pan and subtract what you can reasonably document as discarded.

Recipe nutrition remains an estimate. Ingredient variability, database selection, cooking loss, and scale accuracy all matter. The goal is a transparent method that can be repeated—not a result with unwarranted decimal precision.

Save the ingredient entries, amounts, finished batch weight, and date. The next time you make the recipe, update only what changed. Use the recipe portion calculator when changing the number of servings.
Sources support the factual framework; examples and explanations are original editorial work.

title: How to eat out while working toward your goals | GetMacros
h1: How to eat out while working toward your goals

blocks.text: How to eat out while working toward your goals
You can enjoy a restaurant meal while working on weight loss, muscle gain or everyday nutrition. Start with the whole order and a goal that matters to you.
Build the comparison around your whole order

Start with the exact entrée, then write down each side, sauce and drink you expect to have. Compare that total with another complete order. An entrée-only number can be accurate and still describe only part of your meal.

For example, a hypothetical 450-calorie entrée, 180-calorie side and 120-calorie drink total 750 calories. Replacing the drink with water changes that example to 630; it does not change the entrée’s protein. These figures show the addition, not a published restaurant order.
Check whether the listed nutrition includes dressing, sauce and standard toppings.
Compare meals from the same country’s menu.
Use the restaurant’s calculator for substitutions; do not assume removing a named ingredient subtracts a fixed amount.
Choose a meal that also fits your appetite, preferences and budget.
Compare tracked restaurant meals . Our guides identify calculated combinations and link to the official source so you can check the current order.
Choose what you want from the meal

Are you looking for more protein, a smaller meal, a plant-based option or simply something you enjoy? You do not need to optimize every nutrient at once. A celebration and a quick lunch can involve different choices.
Count the sides, sauces, dressing and drink you expect to have. An entrée’s nutrition is not necessarily the total for its combo meal. Check the named portion and whether dressing is included.
The meal finder compares selected U.S. menu options. It does not cover every item or customization. Use the restaurant’s own menu to confirm current availability, ingredients and nutrition.
Compare grilled and fried versions when both are available.
Ask for a sauce or dressing separately if you want to control the amount.
Choose a drink that fits your preference and meal.
Order a smaller side, share one, or take leftovers home if that suits your appetite.
Add beans or vegetables when you want more fiber.
The size of each difference depends on the restaurant. A salad is not automatically lower in calories, and a sandwich is not automatically a poor choice.
What if the restaurant has no nutrition information?

Choose familiar foods and a portion that feels appropriate. If you track, use a comparable food entry as a rough estimate and accept that it may be off. A palm-sized serving does not always contain the same grams of protein.
You do not need to deliberately overestimate or compensate later. One uncertain meal is not a reason to skip the next one or abandon your routine.
For weight loss or muscle gain

For weight loss, compare portions and calorie-dense additions while keeping the meal satisfying. For muscle gain, check protein and whether the meal supplies enough overall food. A very large order is optional, not a requirement for building muscle.
After eating, return to your usual routine. Judge a plan by the pattern over time, alongside energy, recovery and enjoyment—not by whether one meal matched a calculator exactly.
FDA: understanding the Nutrition Facts label

title: How to Hit Your Protein Goal on a Budget | GetMacros
h1: How to hit your protein goal on a budget

blocks.text: How to hit your protein goal on a budget
Compare the cost per gram of protein, along with portion size and the food you expect to use.

Choose two or three affordable protein anchors, compare them by usable servings or cost per gram of protein, and build repeatable meals around them. Prices vary too much by store and week for one universal cheapest-food ranking.
Start with your target, not a shopping list

A budget plan works better when you know the size of the job. Estimate a reasonable protein target with the free macro calculator or read how much protein you need per day . More is not automatically better, and an inflated target makes every grocery bill harder.

Next, split the target across meals you already eat. Someone aiming for 120 grams could think in four meals of roughly 30 grams, but there is no requirement to make every meal identical. The point is to turn one intimidating daily number into a few shopping decisions.
Use cost per gram without letting it run the whole diet
Package price hides serving size and protein density. Our protein cost per gram calculator uses a simple comparison:

This is useful for comparing two tubs of yogurt, sizes of chicken, cans of fish or powders. It is not a nutrition score. Beans may contribute fiber and carbohydrate; fish may contribute omega-3 fats; dairy may contribute calcium. Cost is one lens.
Eggs, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, canned tuna, tofu
Reduces the cost of last-minute takeout
Dry lentils, beans, chicken thighs, ground turkey, textured vegetable protein
Works across bowls, soups, wraps and pasta
Frozen fish, edamame, cooked beans, portioned meat
Extends shelf life and cuts waste
Milk, soy drink, canned chicken, protein powder when competitively priced
Fills gaps without cooking another meal

USDA resources list beans, lentils, eggs, peanut butter, canned tuna and several frozen or canned meats among practical protein foods. USDA budget guidance also suggests comparing forms and using lower-cost options such as beans, peas and eggs. Local prices still decide the winner.
A shopping method that survives price changes
Check unit price and servings. Compare the shelf label, package weight and edible yield.
Calculate protein value for the close contenders. Do not do this for every food in the building.
Choose foods with multiple uses. A large package is not a deal if half spoils.
Plan the leftovers before buying. Tonight’s chicken can become tomorrow’s wrap; lentils can move from soup to pasta sauce.
Keep one emergency meal. Eggs and toast, tuna pasta, lentil curry or tofu stir-fry can protect both budget and protein target.
Bean-and-meat bowl: combine a smaller portion of meat with beans, rice and vegetables. You get protein from more than one ingredient and stretch the costlier item.
High-protein breakfast: eggs plus yogurt or milk, with oats or toast and fruit.
Pantry pasta: lentil or regular pasta with canned tuna, chicken, beans or textured vegetable protein and tomato sauce.

Fixed “cheapest protein” lists age quickly. Sales, region, dietary restrictions, cooking equipment and package waste all matter. Supplements are not automatically cheaper or more expensive; calculate the actual product. And do not make the entire diet a protein-efficiency contest. Include vegetables, fruit, grains and fats too.

title: How to read a nutrition label | GetMacros
h1: How to read a nutrition label

blocks.text: How to read a nutrition label
Start with the serving size, then check the nutrients in the amount you will eat. This guide follows the U.S. Nutrition Facts label.
Compare the portion, not just the label
Imagine two yogurt labels. These are illustrative numbers, not specific products. Yogurt A lists 120 calories and 12 g protein per 150 g. Yogurt B lists 160 calories and 18 g protein per 200 g.

The lower-calorie label did not mean fewer calories for the portion you wanted. At the same weight, the calories match and B has 2 g more protein. Price, taste and ingredients may still change your choice.
Try this comparison with your own labels . Serving sizes on U.S. labels describe amounts people typically consume; they are not a recommendation for how much you should eat. FDA label guidance .
1. Check the serving and the package

A serving size describes an amount people typically consume; it is not advice about how much you should eat. Check servings per container too. Some labels show both a per-serving column and a whole-package column.
If one serving is 40 g and you eat 60 g, multiply the per-serving numbers by 1.5. For example, 160 calories per serving becomes 240 calories in your portion.
2. Read the nutrients you care about

Calories tell you about energy. Protein, fiber, saturated fat, sodium and added sugar help you understand other parts of the food. There is no single line that decides whether a food belongs in your meals.
Total carbohydrate already includes fiber and sugars. Do not add them again.
Total fat already includes saturated and trans fat.
Added sugars are part of total sugars, not an extra amount on top.
Use protein grams when comparing protein; many labels do not show a protein %DV.
3. Use % Daily Value as a quick guide
The FDA’s rule of thumb is 5% DV or less is low and 20% DV or more is high for a nutrient in one serving. Daily Values are general reference amounts, not your personal targets.
The 2,000-calorie statement provides general nutrition context. It does not mean everyone needs 2,000 calories, or that every Daily Value scales directly with your own calorie intake.
Two products may use different serving sizes. Comparing equal weights helps when the foods serve a similar purpose. Comparing the portions you actually eat may be more useful for planning a meal.
Our food comparison tool offers per-serving, per-100-g and per-100-calorie views. These answer different questions; none is an overall health score.
Ingredients are generally listed from greatest to least weight. Their order does not reveal exact percentages, and a long list is not automatically worse than a short one.
Read the allergen statement and ingredient list if you have an allergy. Do not assume that a missing precautionary warning rules out cross-contact.
Why don’t the numbers always add up?

Nutrition labels use rounding rules. Fiber, sugar alcohols and other ingredients can also affect calorie calculations. Small differences between printed calories and a calculation using 4 calories per gram of protein or carbs and 9 per gram of fat are not automatically errors.
