title: How to set your macros for muscle gain | GetMacros
h1: How to set your macros for muscle gain

blocks.text: How to set your macros for muscle gain
Muscle gain depends on training, enough food and recovery. A useful macro plan supports those things without turning every meal into a calculation.
Do you need a calorie surplus?

A modest surplus can help support muscle gain, especially for experienced lifters. It is not an absolute requirement: some beginners, returning lifters and people with more stored body fat can gain muscle while maintaining or losing weight.

Start with a maintenance estimate. If you choose a surplus, increase food modestly and watch your training, recovery and weight trend. Eating much more does not make muscle grow at the same pace as the scale.

About 1.6–2.2 g/kg/day is a common muscle-building planning range. Research found an average benefit leveling off near 1.6 g/kg, with uncertainty around the estimate. More protein is not guaranteed to produce more muscle.
For a 75 kg person, that planning range is about 120–165 g/day. Split it across meals in whatever pattern is comfortable and practical.
Keep room for carbs and fat
Carbs help fuel demanding training. Rice, oats, potatoes, bread, pasta, beans and fruit are all options. There is no need to treat them as food you must earn.
Fat adds energy and essential fatty acids. The adult reference range is 20–35% of calories. After setting protein and fat, the remaining energy can come from carbs.
An illustrative 2,400-calorie target with 150 g protein and 80 g fat leaves 270 g carbs: 600 + 720 + 1,080 = 2,400 calories. It demonstrates a split, not a target for every lifter.
How do you know whether it is working?

Look at several weeks of training performance, recovery, measurements and weight together. Strength can improve without a matching increase in muscle size, and early weight gain may include water and food in the digestive system.

Muscle-growth rates vary widely. Avoid treating a fixed number of kilograms per month as a promise. If weight is rising faster than intended without useful progress, review the surplus instead of automatically adding more food.
No. Protein powder can make a target easier to reach, but ordinary foods can do the same job. Consistent training and enough total food matter more than a perfectly timed shake.

title: How to set your macros for weight loss | GetMacros
h1: How to set your macros for weight loss

blocks.text: How to set your macros for weight loss
Start with a manageable calorie target, include enough protein, and choose a balance of carbs and fat you can keep eating comfortably.

Weight loss requires an energy deficit over time: using more energy than you take in. Estimate your maintenance calories first. The calculator’s weight-loss option reduces that estimate; it cannot predict your exact rate of loss.
A larger deficit is not automatically better. If you are persistently exhausted, hungry, struggling to recover or becoming distressed about food, reassess the plan.

Adequate protein and resistance training can help preserve muscle during weight loss. People who train often use about 1.6–2.2 g/kg/day as a starting range, but needs vary with body size, health and the size of the deficit.
Use a realistic target, then include protein foods in meals you already eat. A very high target that crowds out other foods is not automatically more effective.

There is no single best macro percentage for weight loss. Carbs can support training and supply fiber; fats provide essential fatty acids and help with vitamin absorption. Choose amounts that leave room for both.
The adult fat reference range is 20–35% of calories. After choosing protein and fat, you can assign the remaining calories to carbs. This is one planning method, not the only way to eat well.

At an illustrative 1,800 calories, 130 g protein provides 520 calories. Choosing 60 g fat provides 540 calories. The remaining 740 calories provide 185 g carbohydrate. These numbers show the calculation; they are not a universal weight-loss plan.
What if your weight is not changing?

Compare several weeks under similar conditions before changing your intake. Water, digestion and menstrual-cycle changes can hide a trend. Check whether portions, drinks, sauces or your activity have changed, rather than assuming your metabolism is broken.

Weight is only one check. Energy, recovery, hunger and whether you can live comfortably with the plan matter too. A qualified clinician or dietitian can help if your situation needs more than a general estimate.
Do carbs have to be low?
No. Lower-carb and lower-fat approaches can both support weight loss. The useful question is which meals help you maintain an appropriate intake while meeting your nutritional needs.

title: What does protein do in your body? | GetMacros
h1: What does protein do in your body?

blocks.text: What does protein do in your body?
Protein helps build and repair tissues, including muscle. Your body also uses it to make enzymes, hormones and antibodies.

Proteins are made from amino acids. Nine are called essential because your body cannot make enough of them; you get them from food. Digestion breaks food proteins into smaller parts that your body can use.
Protein supplies material for muscle repair and growth. Resistance training provides the stimulus. Eating extra protein without suitable training does not have the same effect as combining both.
Your overall daily intake matters more than finding one perfect post-workout food. Meals before and after training can both contribute.

The adult RDA is 0.8 g per kilogram of body weight per day, an amount intended to meet the needs of nearly all healthy adults. Regular exercisers often use a higher range; the ISSN recommends 1.4–2.0 g/kg/day for most exercising individuals.
For a 70 kg adult, those figures are 56 g at the RDA and 98–140 g in the exercise range. They answer different questions. Our daily protein guide explains how to choose a starting point.

Meat, fish, eggs, milk, yogurt, tofu, tempeh, beans and lentils all contribute. Animal proteins and some plant foods, including soy, supply all nine essential amino acids in useful proportions. A varied plant-based diet can also meet protein needs; you do not have to combine particular foods at every meal.
Breakfast: eggs, yogurt or tofu alongside the foods you already enjoy.
Lunch: beans, fish, chicken or tempeh in a sandwich, salad or bowl.
Dinner: a protein food with grains or potatoes and vegetables.
What if you are not getting enough?

Long-term inadequate protein and energy intake can affect health, recovery and muscle maintenance. Tiredness, hair changes or poor recovery alone do not diagnose protein deficiency; they have many possible causes.
If you are losing weight unexpectedly, have persistent symptoms or struggle to eat enough, ask a qualified clinician or dietitian. Do not use a symptom checklist to diagnose yourself.

title: Serving Size vs. Portion Size: What Is the Difference?
h1: Serving size vs. portion size: what is the difference?

blocks.text: Serving size vs. portion size: what is the difference?
A serving size is the standardized amount used on a label. A portion is the amount you actually choose, receive, or eat. Those two amounts can match, but they do not have to.
A 30 g serving, a 45 g portion

Suppose a cereal label lists 150 calories and 4 g protein per 30 g. You pour 45 g. Your multiplier is 45 ÷ 30 = 1.5, so the cereal contributes 225 calories and 6 g protein. Milk, yogurt and toppings are separate.
This arithmetic changes the amount recorded; it does not tell you whether 45 g is right for your appetite. If you use cups instead of weighing food, how tightly it is packed can change the estimate.
Calculate nutrition per recipe portion , or compare two food labels . These sample figures are invented only to demonstrate the calculation, not presented as food data.

On a U.S. Nutrition Facts label, serving size reflects an amount people typically consume; it is not an instruction for how much you should eat. Your portion is personal and situational. A bowl poured at home, a restaurant plate, and a package labeled as two servings can all create different portions from the printed serving.
This matters because every calorie and nutrient number on the label is tied to the stated serving. If your portion is larger or smaller, the numbers scale with it.
Use a ratio, not a guess
Start with the amount you ate and divide it by the labeled serving amount. Then multiply each listed nutrient by that ratio.

If a cereal label lists 40 g and you pour 60 g, the multiplier is 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5. Multiply the calories, protein, carbohydrate, fat, fiber, sodium, and other listed values by 1.5. If you eat half the label serving, multiply by 0.5.
Use the same unit on both sides. Comparing 1 cup eaten with 40 g on the label requires weighing the cup or using a reliable gram equivalent.
Why serving sizes differ between similar foods

FDA regulations use reference amounts customarily consumed, often called RACCs, to set serving-size categories. Product form and packaging can affect what appears on the label. A serving is therefore useful for interpreting that product, but it is not a universal comparison unit across every food.
When two packages list different serving weights, compare nutrients per 100 g, per 100 calories, or per amount you would realistically eat. Each view answers a different question.

Some packages show one column per serving and another for the entire container. This makes the math visible when a package could reasonably be eaten at once. If only a per-serving column is present, check servings per container before assuming the package equals one serving.
A practical way to use the label

First decide what question you have. For sodium or added sugar in the amount you will eat, scale to your portion. For nutrient density, normalize to equal calories or equal grams. For fullness or meal planning, consider the food’s volume, fiber, protein, preparation, and what accompanies it.
A serving size gives you a measurement anchor. It does not judge your appetite, prescribe a meal, or decide whether a food belongs in your diet.

title: What are macros? | GetMacros

blocks.text: Macros are protein, carbohydrates and fat. They provide energy and help your body work. Here is what the numbers mean when you plan a meal.
Builds and repairs tissues; helps make enzymes and antibodies.
Provide energy. Carb-rich foods can also supply fiber.
Provides essential fatty acids and helps absorb vitamins A, D, E and K.
The 4, 4 and 9 figures are useful estimates. Label rounding, fiber and other ingredients can make a food’s printed calories differ slightly from this calculation.

Calories describe how much energy food provides. Macros describe where much of that energy comes from. A calorie target can help with weight planning; looking at protein, carbs and fat can help you choose satisfying meals and support training.
No macro tells the whole story. Fiber, sodium, vitamins, minerals, allergies, cost and the foods you enjoy still matter.
How do you work out your macros?
Estimate your daily calories for your activity and goal.
Choose a protein amount that fits your needs.
Include enough fat, then use carbs for the remaining energy.
The free macro calculator does this arithmetic for you. Its result is a starting estimate, not an exact measurement of your needs.

A sample 2,000-calorie day with 125 g protein and 60 g fat leaves about 240 g carbohydrate: 500 protein calories + 540 fat calories + 960 carbohydrate calories = 2,000. This demonstrates the math; it is not a target for everyone.
Do you need to count macros?

No. You can build meals around protein foods, grains or other carbs, fruit or vegetables, and fats without logging every gram. Tracking can be useful when you have a specific question, such as whether your meals contain enough protein.
You do not need to hit every number exactly. Portions, labels and calorie estimates all have uncertainty. Look for a manageable pattern rather than treating small daily differences as mistakes.

title: What Is a Calorie Deficit? | GetMacros

blocks.text: Understand what a calorie deficit means, how it is estimated and why weight changes over time.

A calorie deficit occurs when average energy intake is below average energy expenditure. It can produce weight loss over time, but the relationship is dynamic: expenditure, body weight, appetite and adherence can change as the plan continues.

Your body uses energy at rest, during movement and exercise, and while processing food. When average intake stays below average expenditure, stored energy helps cover the difference. That is a calorie deficit.

The important word is average . One meal does not create or erase a long-term result. A higher restaurant day can exist inside an overall deficit, just as one low-calorie day cannot guarantee weight loss.
How to estimate a starting deficit
Choose a moderate starting reduction rather than the largest number you can tolerate for a few days.
Keep protein, produce and satisfying meals in the plan.
Track the trend for several weeks under similar conditions.
Adjust only when the trend and adherence both justify it.

The CDC emphasizes gradual, steady weight loss and a broader lifestyle that includes eating patterns, activity, sleep and stress management. A calorie target is one tool inside that process, not the whole process.
Why the simple 3,500-calorie rule falls short

The familiar rule assumes a fixed energy gap produces the same rate forever. Human weight change is not linear. A smaller body generally requires less energy, movement can change, and the body can adapt to prolonged restriction. The NIH Body Weight Planner uses a dynamic model for that reason.
This does not mean a deficit “stops working.” It means the original estimate may no longer describe the current situation.
Signs the plan may be too aggressive
Training performance and recovery decline persistently.
Hunger or fatigue makes the plan difficult to sustain.
Food rules become increasingly rigid or distressing.
The rate of loss is much faster than intended.
Pregnancy, growth, eating-disorder recovery and many medical conditions require individualized care. Speak with a qualified clinician or registered dietitian rather than using a general calculator.
Judge the plan by more than the scale
Use weekly weight trends, but also monitor strength, energy, hunger, sleep and your ability to eat normally around other people. A mathematically larger deficit is not automatically a better plan.

title: What to Eat After a Workout | GetMacros
h1: What to eat after a workout

blocks.text: What to eat after a workout
Plan your next meal around the workout and how soon you will train again.

Eat a useful protein serving and include carbohydrate in proportion to the work you did. If another hard session is only a few hours away, timing becomes more important. Otherwise, a normal meal soon after training is usually a sensible plan.
Build the meal around the recovery job

Post-workout nutrition has three practical jobs: help repair tissue, replace the fuel you used and restore fluid. The size and urgency of each job changes. A casual 40-minute lift followed by a rest day does not require the same recovery plan as a tournament, a long run or two training sessions in one day.
How soon do you need to eat?

The often-repeated “30-minute anabolic window” is too rigid. The ISSN position stand describes a wider practical window and emphasizes the importance of total daily protein. If you ate a mixed meal before training, an immediate snack may be less important.

Timing deserves more attention when recovery time is short. If you must perform hard again within roughly four hours, rapid carbohydrate replacement becomes useful. The ISSN review discusses aggressive carbohydrate intake for this specific situation. That is an athlete-with-another-session problem, not a rule everyone needs after every workout.

Choose a serving that meaningfully contributes to your daily protein target: poultry, fish, lean meat, eggs, dairy, tofu, tempeh, beans or a convenient protein shake. The exact amount depends on body size and the rest of your diet. For most people, consistently reaching an appropriate daily target matters more than chasing a perfect post-workout number.

Use more when the workout was long, glycogen-demanding or followed by another session soon. Rice, potatoes, oats, pasta, bread, fruit, cereal and beans are all workable. A short easy session does not automatically require a large sugar-heavy recovery snack.

Drink according to thirst and the amount you sweated. A normal meal often supplies sodium. People with very high sweat losses, long sessions or repeated work in heat may need a more deliberate plan; the sweat-rate calculator can help estimate fluid loss, but it is not a medical hydration prescription.
Six meals that make the idea concrete
Greek yogurt, oats, berries and milk.
Chicken or tofu, rice, vegetables and a sauce you enjoy.
Lentil pasta with tomato sauce and roasted vegetables.
Turkey or hummus sandwich, fruit and yogurt.
A burrito bowl with rice, beans, meat or sofritas, salsa and guacamole.
A smoothie with milk or soy drink, fruit, oats and protein.
Forgetting to include recovery food in your daily intake. A recovery meal can be part of your target rather than a bonus added on top.
Eating only protein. Carbohydrate has a clear role, especially after demanding endurance or high-volume work.
Using supplements when food would be easier. Shakes are convenient, not mandatory.
Ignoring the full day. Consistent energy, protein and sleep matter beyond one meal.
Use the meal you can repeat. A repeatable routine matters more than one meal.

title: What to Eat Before a Workout | GetMacros
h1: What to eat before a workout

blocks.text: What to eat before a workout
Choose familiar food and a portion that feels comfortable before training.

Start with food you already tolerate. As the workout gets closer, make the meal smaller and easier to digest. Carbohydrate usually does most of the immediate fueling; a moderate protein serving can help you cover your daily target.

If you have two to four hours, eat a normal meal built around carbohydrate, a useful protein source and a portion size you know sits well. If you have less than an hour, a smaller, lower-fat snack is usually easier to tolerate. The “best” choice depends on the workout, the time available and your own gut—not a universal list of approved foods.
A familiar meal with carbs, protein and fluids
Rice with chicken and vegetables; oatmeal, yogurt and fruit; a turkey sandwich with fruit
A smaller mixed snack or light meal
Greek yogurt and a banana; cereal and milk; toast with eggs
Easy-to-digest carbohydrate if you need it
A banana, applesauce, toast, pretzels or a small sports drink
Those are templates, not prescriptions. A large bowl of oatmeal may feel great three hours before lifting and terrible 25 minutes before running. Your previous experience is useful evidence.
Carbs, protein and fat play different roles
Carbohydrate is the most direct training fuel

Hard or long exercise draws heavily on carbohydrate stored as glycogen. The International Society of Sports Nutrition notes that carbohydrate timing matters most when sessions are long, intense or close together. For an ordinary one-hour gym session, you do not need an elaborate loading protocol; arriving generally well-fed is usually enough.
Protein supports the day, not a magic window

A pre-workout protein serving can make it easier to distribute protein across the day. It does not need to be swallowed at an exact minute. A 2017 position stand concludes that total daily protein and reasonably spaced servings matter more than treating the workout as a narrow countdown.
Fat and fiber are useful—but can slow the meal down

Fat and fiber belong in a healthy eating pattern. Close to training, however, a very fatty or very fibrous meal can feel heavy for some people. Reduce them only as much as your comfort and timing require. There is no prize for making every pre-workout meal bland.
Match the food to the session
Strength training: a normal meal in the previous few hours often works. Add a small carb snack if you trained after a long gap and feel flat.
Long endurance work: carbohydrate availability matters more as duration and intensity rise. Practice your strategy before an important event.
Early-morning training: you can train after breakfast or with little food if the session is short and you feel good. If performance drops, test a small carb source rather than forcing a large meal.
Training while cutting: place some of the calories you already planned near the workout instead of automatically adding more.
Training while bulking: the pre-workout meal can help meet a higher calorie target, but leave enough time to digest a larger portion.
Check how long the session will be and how hard you expect to work.
Choose one familiar carbohydrate and one protein source.
Make the portion smaller as the time window shrinks.
Write down how your energy and stomach felt, then adjust one variable next time.
If you routinely feel dizzy, faint, unusually weak or unwell during exercise, stop and seek advice from a qualified clinician. A meal guide cannot diagnose the cause.

title: When Should You Recalculate Calories and Macros? | GetMacros
h1: When should you recalculate calories and macros?

blocks.text: When should you recalculate calories and macros?
Update the target when the inputs or the trend have changed enough to matter.

Recalculate after a meaningful weight change, a sustained change in activity or training, a new goal, or several consistent weeks in which progress differs from the plan. Do not recalculate because of one meal or one weigh-in.
Your target was always an estimate

Calorie equations use current inputs such as weight, height, age and activity. Macro targets then divide that energy estimate according to the goal. If those inputs change, the old result can become less useful.
Body size and composition influence energy expenditure.
A new job, step count or training schedule can change daily expenditure.
Maintenance, cutting and gaining require different energy directions.
A consistent trend can show that the starting estimate needs adjustment.
Illness, injury or a return to training can change needs and priorities.
What does not justify a new target?
One unexpectedly high or low weigh-in.
A few days of soreness or appetite change.
A calculator giving a slightly different answer after rounding.
Changing the target too often makes it impossible to learn from the plan. Hold a reasonable target steady long enough to see a trend.
Compare weekly weight averages for at least two to three weeks.
Check training performance, hunger, energy and adherence.
Confirm that activity has not changed accidentally.
If the trend is consistently wrong for the goal, adjust modestly.
Run the calculator again after a meaningful change in body weight or routine.
Why needs can fall during weight loss

A smaller body generally uses less energy, and research also describes adaptive reductions in energy expenditure during prolonged restriction and weight loss. The size of that adaptation varies. It should not be used to declare a metabolism “broken,” but it is another reason an old maintenance estimate may stop matching current data.

Keep protein relatively stable unless body size, training or clinical advice changes the target. Most routine adjustments can come from carbohydrate and fat according to preference and training needs.

title: Why Did I Gain Weight Overnight? | GetMacros
h1: Why did I gain weight overnight?

blocks.text: Why did I gain weight overnight?
The scale can change quickly because it measures everything in your body—not only fat.

A one-day increase usually reflects a mixture of fluid, food and waste in the digestive system, carbohydrate storage and normal measurement noise. Look at a trend under similar conditions before changing your plan.
The scale measures more than body fat

Your scale reports total mass at one moment. That includes body tissue, water, glycogen, food moving through your digestive tract and waste. Several of those can change within hours. Body-fat change is much slower than the dramatic overnight jumps that make people want to rewrite an entire diet.
Six common reasons the number moved
A later or larger meal has physical mass while it is being digested. The scale sees it even before absorption matters.
A salty restaurant day can change thirst and fluid balance. A kidney review describes short-term body-weight increases after abrupt increases in sodium intake.
Carbohydrate is stored as glycogen. Glycogen status and body water are related, although the exact relationship is more complicated than a fixed water-per-gram rule.
Hard or unfamiliar exercise can temporarily shift fluid as tissue responds and recovers.
Different bowel and bladder timing can move the number without saying anything useful about fat loss.
Menstrual-cycle-related fluid changes can affect scale weight. Individual patterns vary.
What to do the morning after
Do not compensate with an extreme restriction day. Return to your normal plan.
Use the same measuring conditions. A common approach is morning, after using the bathroom and before eating, with similar clothing.
Watch a rolling trend. Compare several weeks, not one Tuesday with one Wednesday.
Add context. Note unusually salty meals, travel, hard training, menstrual-cycle timing or a late dinner.
Adjust only when the trend supports it. If the average is moving away from your goal for multiple weeks, then review intake, activity and adherence.

Imagine your morning weights are 172.1, 171.8, 172.4, 171.9, 174.0, 172.6 and 172.2 pounds. The 174-pound reading looks dramatic by itself. In the context of the week, it looks like a brief spike that returned toward the established range. That pattern calls for observation, not punishment.
Weekly averages are not magic either. They simply reduce the power of a noisy reading. Compare averages taken with the same method and pay attention to the direction over enough time to matter.
When an increase deserves medical attention

Rapid weight gain accompanied by swelling, shortness of breath, chest symptoms or a new medical concern should not be treated as a routine diet fluctuation. Contact a qualified clinician promptly. Certain heart, kidney, liver, hormonal and medication-related issues can affect fluid balance, and a website cannot sort those out safely.

If your plan is designed for fat loss, one higher restaurant meal does not erase it. If your plan is designed for muscle gain, a lower morning reading does not prove the bulk failed. Use the weight-goal timeline calculator for a broad planning estimate, then judge real progress by the trend and by outcomes you care about—training, measurements, energy and consistency.
